end.question: Hydrogen fluoride (HF) boils at 19.5 °C and hydrogen chloride (HCl) at −85 °C, although HCl is the heavier molecule. What is the main reason?

options.label: HF molecules form hydrogen bonds with one another
HF molecules are larger than HCl molecules
HF has a stronger covalent bond inside the molecule

end.explanation: Hydrogen on a highly electronegative atom like fluorine is drawn to a lone pair on the next molecule, a hydrogen bond, which beats the extra dispersion force of the heavier HCl.

end.question: Pulling a mole of liquid ethanol's molecules apart takes 38.6 kJ, and breaking the C–C bond in a mole of ethanol takes 348 kJ. What happens when ethanol boils?

options.label: The molecules separate and stay whole
The C–C bonds break and the pieces drift off
Both the molecules and their bonds separate

end.explanation: The heat only has to overcome the much weaker forces between molecules, so boiling leaves each molecule intact.

end.question: A diagram shows a sodium ion in water with the oxygen ends of the water molecules pointing at the ion. Which force does it show?
end.explanation: The negative ends of the polar water molecules point at the positive ion: an ion–dipole force.

problems.question: Which of these molecules can form hydrogen bonds with others of its own kind?
problems.explanation: In methanol a hydrogen is attached to oxygen, so it can be drawn to a lone pair on the next molecule. The other three have no H on N, O or F.

problems.question: Fluorine (F₂) is a gas at room temperature and iodine (I₂) is a solid. Both are nonpolar. What explains the difference?

options.label: Iodine's larger electron cloud is more polarizable, so its dispersion forces are stronger
Fluorine has a stronger bond than iodine

problems.explanation: Bigger electron clouds are easier to distort, so heavier nonpolar molecules attract their neighbours more strongly.
